summary: Jacob leaves Laban with his family and possessions, and a divine dream restrains Laban when he pursues. They establish a boundary by oath and a heap of stones; Jacob then reconciles with Esau, settles in the region, and regularly supplies Isaac and Rebecca, while the narrator recalls the land's former giant inhabitants.
whyItMatters: The return promised to Jacob advances through restrained conflict, sworn boundaries, and care for his parents. The account also embeds his journey in a morally charged history of the land's earlier inhabitants.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: The route from Laban's flocks to Gilead, the Jabbok, and the Jordan region, with Isaac and Rebecca living at Abraham's tower near Hebron.
context.literaryForm: Journey and treaty narrative with a geographical excursus and notices of household support.

before.text: Laban has become envious of Jacob's increasing possessions and has taken sheep back. Jacob's departure now answers that worsening situation.

here.text: The pursuit ends in an oath against hostile crossing, after which Jacob reconnects with Esau and provides for his parents.

after.text: Jacob's household reaches the area of Shechem, where Dinah's assault is followed by the city's destruction and a long legal interpretation.

outline.heading: Departure and pursuit
outline.note: Leah and Rachel agree to go; Jacob hides his intention, and a dream restrains Laban.

outline.heading: A boundary oath and witness
outline.note: A feast and heap memorialize the agreement against hostile crossing.

outline.heading: The earlier inhabitants of Gilead
outline.note: The narrator describes giants, their territories, and a divine judgment on their deeds.

outline.heading: Reconciliation and settlement
outline.note: Laban leaves, Esau reconciles with Jacob, and Jacob crosses the Jordan.

outline.heading: Provision for Isaac and Rebecca
outline.note: Regular gifts and family background explain the parents’ residence and their blessing of Jacob.

keyVerses.text: And on the fifteenth of those days Jacob made a feast for Laban, and for all who came with him, and Jacob sware to Laban that day, and Laban also to Jacob, that neither should cross the mountain of Gilead to the other with evil purpose.
keyVerses.why: The sworn prohibition concerns crossing with evil intent, defining the peace agreed by Jacob and Laban.

keyVerses.text: And he passed over the Jabbok in the ninth month, on the eleventh thereof. And on that day Esau, his brother, came to him, and he was reconciled to him, and departed from him unto the land of Seir, but Jacob dwelt in tents.
keyVerses.why: The chapter records reconciliation with Esau briefly before the family’s later conflicts.

keyVerses.text: And thither Jacob sent all that he did send to his father and his mother from time to time, all they needed, and they blessed Jacob with all their heart and with all their soul.
keyVerses.why: Material provision for his parents closes the chapter with their wholehearted blessing.

questions.question: Do Leah and Rachel agree to leave?
questions.answer: Jacob tells them about the dream directing his return and speaks kindly to them. They say they will go wherever he goes, although he conceals the plan from Laban.

questions.question: Why does Laban not injure Jacob?
questions.answer: The narrator attributes his restraint to the Lord appearing to him in a dream. The chapter does not reproduce that dream's words, so its content should not be filled in from another version of the story.

questions.question: What is the “Heap of Witness”?
questions.answer: It is the heap Jacob makes to memorialize the mutual oath after their feast. The agreement forbids either party from crossing the mountain toward the other with evil purpose, rather than banning every journey across it.

questions.question: Who are the Rephaim in this chapter?
questions.answer: The narrator describes them as former giant inhabitants of Gilead and lists their territories and royal centers. These are claims within the work's account of the land's past; the chapter provides no independent evidence with which to verify their size or history.

questions.question: How should the destruction of the former inhabitants be understood?
questions.answer: The text attributes their destruction to God because of their evil and also condemns the Amorites who replaced them. That severe narrative judgment should not be converted into a license to remove populations or assign collective guilt today.

questions.question: How much does the chapter say about Jacob and Esau’s reconciliation?
questions.answer: It gives a date and says Esau came, was reconciled, and departed to Seir. It does not narrate the conversation or motives, so the guide should leave those details open.

questions.question: Why list food and seasonal gifts sent to the parents?
questions.answer: The list makes Jacob's continuing support concrete despite living apart from Isaac and Rebecca. The closing explanation contrasts their residence at Abraham's tower with Esau's move to Seir and ends with the parents blessing Jacob.

glossary.def: The named stone heap marking the agreement that Jacob and Laban will not cross toward one another with hostile intent.
The earlier inhabitants of Gilead whom this account describes as giants.
Units of length used in the narrator’s description of the giants; no modern conversion is supplied here.
